title: Ichthyosis Vulgaris

steps.tx: **Ichthyosis vulgaris** represents the most frequent inherited disorder of keratinisation, affecting approximately one in two hundred and fifty individuals as an autosomal semidominant trait. Loss-of-function mutations in the filaggrin gene on chromosome 1q21 disrupt epidermal barrier formation. Patients present in early childhood with fine, translucent, polygonal scales that predominantly cover extensor extremities while strictly sparing the flexural creases. Associated findings include prominent hyperlinear palms and soles, keratosis pilaris, and atopic eczema. Skin biopsy demonstrates marked attenuation or total absence of the epidermal granular layer.
steps.say: Ichthyosis vulgaris is an autosomal semidominant condition resulting from filaggrin gene mutations. Fine pale scales coat extensor surfaces like the shins, but crucially spare the antecubital and popliteal fossae. Look for palmar hyperlinearity and keratosis pilaris. On histology, the hallmark diagnostic feature is an absent or markedly reduced stratum granulosum.

vis.title: Ichthyosis Vulgaris Profile
rows: Extensor extremities with classic flexural sparing
Markedly attenuated or completely absent on biopsy

steps.tx: **X-linked ichthyosis** arises from steroid sulfatase enzyme deficiency caused by deletions or point mutations in the STS gene at chromosome Xp22.3. Male infants present within the first three months of life with dark brown, tightly adherent, polygonal scales distributed over the limbs, trunk, and characteristically covering the lateral neck in a dirty neck pattern. Unlike ichthyosis vulgaris, flexural creases are often involved while palms and soles are spared. Asymptomatic comma-shaped corneal deposits occur in fifty percent of adult males. Cryptorchidism occurs in up to twenty percent.
steps.say: X-linked ichthyosis stems from steroid sulfatase deficiency and affects males. It manifests with dirty-brown polygonal scales that prominently encircle the lateral neck while sparing palms and soles. Corneal opacities seen on slit lamp examination do not affect vision. Obstetric history often reveals failure of labor progression due to placental sulfatase deficiency.

vis.alt: Medical illustration of X-linked ichthyosis with dark brown adherent scales.
vis.caption: Dark brown polygonal scales along the neck and trunk with retention hyperkeratosis. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: **Lamellar ichthyosis** is a severe autosomal recessive non-bullous disorder of cornification most commonly caused by pathogenic variants in the TGM1 gene encoding transglutaminase-1. Most affected neonates present at birth encased in a taut, shiny collodion membrane. Following membrane shedding, patients develop universal, large, dark brown, quadrangular plate-like scales over the entire body surface without sparing flexures. Cicatricial ectropion, eclabium, scarring alopecia, and heat intolerance from severe hypohidrosis constitute major clinical complications. Topical urea, alpha-hydroxy acids, and oral acitretin improve shedding.
steps.say: Lamellar ichthyosis is an autosomal recessive condition commonly linked to transglutaminase-1 defects. Newborns usually present encased in a collodion shell. Once desquamated, dark plate-like scales involve the entire skin including flexural creases. Severe ectropion risks exposure keratitis, and defective sweat ducts cause potentially life-threatening hyperthermia in hot conditions.

vis.alt: Illustration of lamellar ichthyosis showing plate-like scales.
vis.caption: Large plate-like polygonal scales across the body with severe ectropion and eclabium. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: **Collodion baby** describes a striking neonatal presentation in which the infant is born encased in a shiny, taut, parchment-like membrane that distorts facial anatomy, producing severe ectropion and eclabium. The collodion jacket fissures and peels over two to four weeks. Most cases eventually declare themselves as lamellar ichthyosis or congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma, though ten percent resolve permanently as self-healing collodion baby. Immediate management in a high-humidity incubator with sterile barrier ointments prevents hypothermia, transcutaneous fluid loss, and fatal neonatal sepsis.
steps.say: A collodion baby is born inside a tight glistening membrane that restricts chest movement and feeding. Crucial management in the neonatal unit requires humidified incubators and bland barrier ointments. Keratolytic agents such as salicylic acid must never be applied because thin neonatal skin permits rapid toxic systemic absorption.

nodes.label: Humidified Incubator
nodes.sub: Sterile fluid balance and bland emollients

steps.tx: **Harlequin ichthyosis** represents the most catastrophic congenital disorder of cornification, transmitted as an autosomal recessive condition due to loss-of-function mutations in the ABCA12 lipid transporter gene. Neonates are encased in massive, thick, yellow-white diamond-shaped armour plates separated by wide, fiery red fissures. Severe bilateral ectropion, absence of external ear structures, eclabium, and digital gangrene from constriction bands are typical. Prompt admission to the neonatal intensive care unit and immediate initiation of oral acitretin has transformed this previously fatal disease into a survivable condition.
steps.say: Harlequin ichthyosis is caused by homozygous ABCA12 mutations disabling epidermal glucosylceramide export. Massive keratin armour plates with deep erythematous fissures leave the infant at severe risk of sepsis and hypothermia. Early oral acitretin accelerates plate shedding and dramatically enhances neonatal survival.

vis.alt: Illustration of harlequin ichthyosis neonatal clinical features.
vis.caption: Thick plate-like hyperkeratotic armour with deep fissures, severe ectropion, and eclabium. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: **Epidermolysis bullosa** encompasses a group of inherited mechanobullous disorders marked by profound tissue fragility where minimal frictional shearing provokes blisters and erosions. Classification hinges on the ultrastructural level of cleavage: simplex within basal keratinocytes from keratin 5 or 14 defects; junctional through the lamina lucida from laminin-332 or collagen XVII mutations; and dystrophic beneath the lamina densa due to type VII collagen (COL7A1) mutations. Recessive dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa leads to pseudosyndactyly mitten deformities and high lifetime mortality from aggressive metastatic squamous cell carcinoma.
steps.say: Epidermolysis bullosa causes blistering following trivial mechanical friction. Subtype classification relies on the level of split: simplex occurs in the basal layer, junctional occurs within the basement membrane lamina lucida, and dystrophic occurs in the sublamina densa. Recessive dystrophic disease causes devastating hand pseudosyndactyly and early aggressive skin malignancies.

vis.alt: Illustration of epidermolysis bullosa cleavage planes.
vis.caption: Intraepidermal blister cleavage plane within basal keratinocytes following minor friction. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: **Neurofibromatosis type 1** is an autosomal dominant neurocutaneous syndrome caused by heterozygous mutations in the NF1 gene on chromosome 17q11.2, which encodes the tumour suppressor protein neurofibromin. Clinical diagnosis requires meeting two or more cardinal criteria: six or more cafe-au-lait macules exceeding five millimetres before puberty or fifteen millimetres after puberty; intertriginous axillary or inguinal freckling known as Crowe sign; two or more cutaneous neurofibromas or one plexiform neurofibroma; optic pathway glioma; two or more iris Lisch nodules; and distinctive osseous sphenoid dysplasia.
steps.say: Neurofibromatosis type 1 results from NF1 mutations leading to unrestrained RAS activation. Remember the classic diagnostic criteria: six cafe-au-lait macules, Crowe sign axillary freckling, cutaneous neurofibromas, optic pathway gliomas, and iris Lisch nodules on slit lamp examination. Plexiform neurofibromas carry an eight to twelve percent lifetime risk of malignant transformation.

steps.tx: **Tuberous sclerosis** complex is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by inactivating mutations in TSC1 (hamartin on chromosome 9q34) or TSC2 (tuberin on chromosome 16p13.3), leading to continuous hyperactivation of the mTOR growth cascade. Cardinal cutaneous signs include three or more hypomelanotic ash-leaf macules visible under Wood lamp, facial angiofibromas (adenoma sebaceum) across the nose and cheeks, periungual Koenen tumours emerging around puberty, and leathery lumbosacral shagreen patches. Associated systemic hamartomas include cortical tubers causing epilepsy, subependymal giant cell astrocytomas, cardiac rhabdomyomas, and renal angiomyolipomas.
steps.say: Tuberous sclerosis stems from mutations in hamartin or tuberin disinhibiting mTOR signalling. Hypopigmented ash-leaf macules are the earliest detectable cutaneous sign, best visualized under Wood lamp illumination. Malar angiofibromas and subungual Koenen tumours develop during childhood. Systemic monitoring focuses on seizure control and screening for renal angiomyolipomas and cardiac rhabdomyomas.

vis.alt: Illustration of tuberous sclerosis complex clinical features.
vis.caption: Characteristic cutaneous signs of tuberous sclerosis complex including hypomelanotic macules and facial angiofibromas. Illustration: StewardMD original.
